rv.q: It’s not Sondheim at his greatest, but it’s still uniquely him: witty, wry and suddenly wise.
Sure, it’s no masterpiece, but a minor-league swansong from a giant of musicals is still a major deal.
The musical fantasy that unfolds on the National’s Lyttelton stage is, for long stretches, utterly absorbing.
It's not neat, arguably it's not even finished, and yet Are breathes a remarkable sense of life.
Are is a really, really great example of half a musical.
It's flip, funny, and undeniably stylish. But essentially unsatisfying, too.
It is full of adventurous imagination, with some signature Sondheim sparks, but the trouble spots are still clear to see.
Because Are is extremely sketchy and gets lumpier and messier as it goes on.
Overall, I'd say this brokenback show is for Sondheim completists only.

But for all the polish of Mantello’s staging, this really just feels like a purposeless waste of time – an experiment that should have stayed in its masterly creator’s bottom drawer.
Like so much Sondheim, the show makes demands on an audience - but "not demands you can't meet," as an earlier lyric from the same composer (in Merrily Along) puts it.

Are opened Off Broadway in 2023 and now makes its UK debut at the National, a witty, dreamlike, insightful, sometimes maddening, ultimately moving tribute to the man who left an indelible mark on musical theatre.
It feels like a late-career bonus, a curiosity but one that gleams.
Not at the top of the Sondheim oeuvre, Are is enjoyable, fun, stylishly staged.

At its worst David Ives' book is a single punchline Monty Python sketch dragged out into an entire musical.
It may not be the swan song we wanted, but it’s the end of an era for sure.
You can never accuse Stephen Sondheim of being boring in his lifetime, and Are is a fitting addition to his legacy.

The first half is pure fun: greeted at The Everything Cafe with a cooing “your enabler will be here momentarily” the five are offered a vast menu but immediately met with a magnificently operatic aria from the waiter about how everything is off tonight.
Still, Ives’s terrific book has turned Buñuel’s films into an evening that is not only eerily modern, but reflective of our seemingly pre-apocalyptic times.
The second act becomes increasingly abstract, with characters mired in repetitive existential debates that sap the show of its initial spark.
Are is enlivened by a terrific ensemble, Joe Mantello's superb staging, and David Zinn's lavish set.

cn.t: Sondheim's unfinished final work divides critics with its surrealist take on Buñuel films—praised for a brilliant cast and inventive staging, but faulting an uneven structure, sparse second-act music, and repetitive satire of the wealthy.
